output.headline: A milder winter could mean a good year for Auckland’s bees, experts say
output.standfirst: One researcher says New Zealand’s mild winter has let bee colonies build up strength early, even as Auckland beekeepers field a record number of calls to clear swarms from cars and city streets
output.bodyHtml:
A milder than usual winter has helped New Zealand’s bees build up their numbers earlier and in greater strength this spring, one ecologist says, describing it as a good sign for this year’s bee populations – even as the resulting swarms engulf parked cars and blanket inner-city street signs across Auckland, the country’s largest city.

The Auckland Beekeepers Association is fielding five to 10 calls a day for help removing swarms, with individual members also contacted directly for assistance.

“In past years, it was under five a day,” said Bryan Lang, the association’s swarm control coordinator, adding the team has now dealt with at least 100 call-outs.

In October, a swarm plastered the back of a parked car in Birkenhead for two hours according to witnesses. A woman inside was napping at the time, Lang understands.

“I’m surprised she didn’t hear them because they’re pretty loud,” he said.

Related: The night-sky image so incredible the NZ man behind it has been accused of using AI

A month earlier, a swarm took over a sign at a busy intersection on Auckland’s major commercial thoroughfare, Queen Street, forcing pedestrians to reroute.

Bee colonies swarm during spring and early summer, when part of a colony that has outgrown its hive leaves in search of a new home or extra food, while scout bees search for a suitable dwelling.

“As a beekeeper, you don’t want them to swarm because you’re losing two-thirds of your bees, and right at the time when they should be bringing honey in for you,” said Lang. “And it’s not great for your neighbours either.”

Public awareness about why bees swarm, and what to do if one takes over a garden or street, is growing, with many turning to social media bee-swarming pages and local beekeeping clubs for help, Lang said.

The association’s president, Ken Brown, says bee swarms in the countryside go largely unnoticed, but “townies” are less familiar with them.

“If you don’t know about bees – how they’re only defensive – then you might be intimidated with thousands of venomous insects flying around,” he said, adding that a colony of bees is at its most placid when swarming.

Brown attributes the shift to a much milder winter and start to spring, which led bees to swarm weeks earlier than usual and in larger numbers as colonies split. New Zealand had its third warmest winter on record in 2026, according to Earth Sciences NZ, with other parts of the world – including in North America – seeing similar shifts in bee behaviour as global warming leads to hotter winters and springs.

“Beekeeping is much more unpredictable nowadays because you do have the extremes of weather and the different patterns. Every year is slightly different, but it’s actually even more different in recent times,” said Brown.

Milder temperatures over winter can mean a colony develops a larger brood of eggs, larvae and pupae. Provided they avoid the deadly varroa mite parasite, the survivors emerge “much stronger and ready to swarm sooner”, said Brown.

Prof Phil Lester, an etymologist and ecologist at Victoria University, said beekeepers have also been busy catching swarms elsewhere in the country, including in Wellington.

Unmanaged bee swarms that cannot be captured do carry some risk: they may spread the varroa mite to other honeybees or native bees, and cost beekeepers hives just as they are gearing up for honey production.

Still, it could be a positive signal for this year’s bee populations, Lester said.

“It means they have been able to build up numbers and populations, earlier than perhaps they normally would do … its probably a good indication that it is a good bee year.”
